title: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook, Appendix C: How to Write a Good Requirement
source: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook, NASA/SP-2016-6105 Rev 2, Appendix C "How to Write a Good Requirement" (checklists C.1 to C.4), web edition last updated 26 July 2023, read 2026-10-08.

rules.text: Shall marks a requirement, will a fact or a declaration of purpose, should a goal.
A requirement names who or what acts, in the active voice: the product shall do, perform, provide or weigh something.
Performance and other quantitative values carry their tolerances (less than, at least, plus or minus).
A requirement says what is needed, not how to provide it, and is not a description of an operation.
A requirement is stated positively rather than with shall not; the check reports a negative as a warning.
TBD values are few; a best estimate marked TBR is preferred, and each names what closes it, who closes it and by when.
Each requirement comes with a rationale, and its assumptions are stated.
A requirement has no ambiguous terms such as as appropriate, etc., and/or, or but not limited to.
One thought per requirement statement: two requirements are not joined in one sentence.
A requirement uses no indefinite pronoun such as this or these.
Every requirement is uniquely numbered so another document can refer to it.
Every requirement can be verified by test, demonstration, inspection or analysis, and says which.

A requirement has none of the unverifiable terms flexible, easy, sufficient, safe, ad hoc, adequate, accommodate, user-friendly, usable, when required, if required, appropriate, fast, portable, light-weight, small, large, maximize, minimize, robust, quickly, easily or clearly.
Other vague words ending in -ly or -ize are avoided as well.
Every incomplete requirement is captured as a TBD or TBR, and all of them are kept in one list with the requirements.
Terms are used the same way throughout and the key ones are defined.
Requirements hold no personnel or task assignments; deliveries and duties belong in the statement of work.
